newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexicans wonder if Salinas next in Colosio probe.
newsitem.headline: Mexicans wonder if Salinas next in Colosio probe.

text.p: The questioning of a top aide to ex-Mexican President Carlos Salinas this week in the murder probe of a leading politician has led to speculation here that the disgraced former leader may himself testify.

Mexican authorities said late on Friday they had questioned Jose Cordoba Montoya, the right hand man to Salinas during his 1988-1994 presidency, about the 1994 assassination of ruling party presidential candidate Luis Donaldo Colosio.

In a brief statement, the Attorney General's office said Cordoba was called in "to respond to an ample interrogation." Officials have said in the past they do not consider Cordoba a suspect in the case.

But two-and-a-half years after the killing, the questioning of Salinas' ex-chief of staff is sure to increase suspicion among Mexicans that the pair had something to do with the murder, Mexico's worst political crime in decades.

Both Cordoba and Salinas have repeatedly said they had nothing to do with the assassination of Colosio, who as standard bearer of the long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) was almost certain to win the presidency.
"Is it Carlos Salinas' turn to testify to the Attorney General's office?" asked Mexico City's influential Reforma newspaper in an editorial on Saturday.
"If (Cordoba's) questioning marks a new turn in the case, the man now living in Ireland will have to provide whatever information he can to clear up the case," the newspaper wrote.

Salinas fled Mexico in early 1995 when a peso devaluation shortly after the end of his term sparked an economic crisis and questions arose about corruption in his administration. After reportedly spending some time in the United States, Canada and Cuba, Salinas has said he now lives in Dublin.

Mexico's government insists a conspiracy was behind the killing of Colosio, gunned down during a campaign rally in the northern border city of Tijuana in March 1994. Polls show most Mexicans believe the murder was a plot by PRI hardliners who did not want the reform-minded Colosio to take office.

After accusations he was linked to PRI hardliners and tried to get Colosio to step down as candidate, the French-born Cordoba earlier this year proclaimed his innocence and said he was ready to testify at any time in the case.
Officials questioned Cordoba on Wednesday, seven months after he first tried to clear his name, but did not disclose the news to the media until late on Friday.
Cordoba, who served as an advisor to the World Bank after the Salinas term, was questioned for 21 hours by investigators and asked about 200 questions, Reforma said.
Reforma said Cordoba denied there was ever a reported break between Salinas and the man he handpicked to be his successor. He also said Colosio had never been asked to step down as candidate.

Only confessed gunman Mario Aburto has been convicted and a host of special prosecutors in the case have unsuccessfully tried to untangle what is believed to be a web of political intrigue at the highest levels of government.

Former Tijuana police chief Federico Benitez, who carried out his own probe of the case, and a series of other people close to the case have been murdered since the assassination, fuelling speculation of a conspiracy.

Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo, who took Colosio's place as candidate, has made solving the case one of the priorities of his term and has promised that officials will question anyone they need to in order to solve the case.
